Chapter 4: Speaking to Shared Interests—Communicating in Ways That Resonate
Let’s take a closer look at what really makes communication click. It’s not just about saying things clearly—it’s about making your message actually matter to someone else.
The most powerful messages? They’re the ones that tap into the listener’s own interests, values, and real-life experiences.
Instead of thinking, “Here’s what I want,” imagine flipping your approach. What if you started from, “Here’s why this matters to you”?
When you frame a conversation around the other person’s perspective, suddenly it’s more engaging—and honestly, a lot more persuasive.
Let’s say you’re in a business negotiation. It’s tempting to just focus on your own goals. But here’s the thing: it’s usually much more effective to show how your idea benefits the other party. Maybe you address their worries, connect your proposal to their goals, or help them solve a problem they actually care about.
And this idea isn’t just for boardrooms or big deals. In your personal relationships, thinking about shared interests can help you avoid all sorts of misunderstandings and unnecessary conflict.
When you acknowledge how someone else is feeling and what’s truly important to them, your conversations become a lot more productive—and way less confrontational.
So, how do you actually put this into practice? Here are a few ways:
Talk about what matters to the other person, not just yourself. Ask good questions to really get at their priorities and concerns. And when you’re making suggestions, try to frame them in a way that lines up with what they value.
Sure, this approach takes some empathy and flexibility. It’s about meeting people where they are, rather than expecting them to come to you.
But over time, you’ll notice something powerful: this habit builds trust, and makes it so much easier to find common ground.
